title: How do you deliver a 60-second recommendation at the end of a case?
description: The last 60 seconds are what the interviewer remembers and writes up. What to do, what to say, and the mistake to avoid.
hook: The recommendation is the last thing the interviewer hears, and it shapes how they remember the whole case. Here is how to give one that is short, clear and confident.
body:
Stage 9 of 10 in the ten stages of a case.

Why it matters

The last 60 seconds are what the interviewer remembers and writes up.

The common mistake

Replaying the whole case from the start instead of giving the answer.

What to do, and what to say

Answer first

Prepare for 20 seconds, speak for about 60: recommendation, 2-3 reasons with numbers, risks, next steps.

"I recommend entering through a joint venture. Two reasons: the market grows 12% a year, and a partner caps our investment at $20M with breakeven in year 2. The key risk is depending on the partner, so as next steps I’d agree exit terms and test demand in one city."

Park what you didn’t cover

Branches you never reached belong in next steps. It shows you tracked the whole problem.

"...and as a next step I’d also look at the cost side, which we didn’t get to today."

Practise the moment

Read the situation and say your answer out loud before you open the model.

The interviewer says: "The CEO walks in. What do you tell her?"

Show a strong answer

"I recommend X. Two reasons: [reason with a number], and [reason with a number]. The main risk is Y, so as next steps I’d Z."

Why it works: Answer first, reasons with numbers, risk, next steps, in about 60 seconds.

You never got to the cost side of your structure. Where does it go?

Show a strong answer

In next steps: "...and I’d also look at the cost side, which we didn’t get to today."

Why it works: It shows you tracked the whole problem.

Next stage: throughout the case.

Put the recommendation under a stress test

Before speaking, ask: "If the interviewer challenges my biggest assumption, can I defend the choice?" Suppose the suggested expansion depends on gaining 5% market share. Be prepared to explain what acquisition channel, competitive advantage or pilot data supports that share, and what you would do if the attainable share were only 2%.

A recommendation should not pretend uncertainty vanished. Give the best supported decision now, cite the quantitative reasons, name the risk that could overturn it and specify the next validation step. That is more useful than saying "the client should analyse further" without making a choice.
